title: Bamiyan remembered
hookLine: the empty niches in the cliff where the great Buddhas stood

cards: A tall arch is cut deep into a honey-colored cliff. It's the shape of a standing figure, but there's no figure in it. Just rock, scarred and hollow, with small caves around it where people once lived and prayed.
Farther along the cliff, another arch, another emptiness. Below, fields and poplar trees, and children walking to school. The cliff is in Afghanistan, in the valley of Bamiyan.
Today we sit with what used to stand there.

teach.b: Long ago, great standing Buddhas were carved into that cliff, looking out over a valley on old trade routes. Monks lived in the caves around them, and travelers and pilgrims passed through and wrote about what they saw.

Long after the valley's people had become Muslim, the statues stayed, part of the landscape and of local memory. Then the Taliban government of the time declared them idols and destroyed them with explosives.
People from around the world and from different faiths, Muslims among them, spoke out against it.
What was left were the empty niches. Since then, a long debate.
Some want to rebuild the Buddhas. Some say the niches should stay empty, as a witness to what happened. Once, an image of a Buddha was projected into a niche in light.
Bamiyan raises a sharp Buddhist question: what is lost when a statue is lost? Images of the Buddha are deeply honored; people bow, offer flowers, and some speak of feeling the Buddha near.
Yet the old texts tell of a monk named Vakkali, sick and near death, who longed to look at the Buddha's body one more time.

At his bedside, the Buddha asked what good it would do to see this decaying body: whoever sees the teaching sees him, and whoever sees him sees the teaching. So the niches can be read two ways at once.
They are a real loss, and grief for them makes sense. And what the statues pointed to, the teaching, did not fall with the stone.

how: Buddhists and others remember Bamiyan in talks, exhibitions and visits to the valley, and the question of whether to rebuild the statues or leave the niches empty is still discussed among scholars, local people and heritage bodies.

games.why: people still debate rebuilding versus leaving the niches empty, and once an image of a Buddha was projected into one with light.

practice: Rest your eyes on an empty space near you, an empty chair, a doorway, the space between your hands, or close them and feel the quiet room around you.

Notice the urge to fill it with a thought, a plan, a song, and let the urge pass; if something you've lost comes to mind, let it sit there with you a while. The emptiness can hold grief and calm at once.

wordCard.voice: Bamiyan remembered. The valley in Afghanistan where great Buddhas stood in the cliff, and where the empty niches still remind people of what was there. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit buddha: the awakened one, whose great images stood in the cliff at Bamiyan.

carryVoice: Your line: the empty niches. The stone fell, but the teaching didn't fall with it. See you tomorrow.
